opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they're useful because they're the closest precedents we have for technologies that are both dual-use and potentially catastrophic at scale. AI isn't just another consumer technology like smartphones or social media. It has economic upside, military applications, and the potential for mass-casualty misuse. That combination is what CBRN technologies, chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, have in common, and over the decades we've built up a fair amount of strategic thinking about how states handle them.

Each analogy highlights something different. With nuclear, the relevant lesson is deterrence. During the Cold War you got mutual assured destruction, where neither side could make a decisive first move without inviting a devastating response. I think there's an analogous dynamic emerging with AI, something like mutual assured AI malfunction: if one state looks like it's about to gain a unilateral, destabilizing advantage, say by racing toward superintelligence it might lose control of, rivals have both the incentive and, increasingly, the means to sabotage that project, through cyberattacks, degrading data centers, and so on. That threat of sabotage can create a kind of deterrent equilibrium.

Nuclear also gives us nonproliferation. We put a lot of effort into making sure fissile material and weapons designs don't end up with rogue actors or terrorists. The AI analog is compute security and export controls, tracking where advanced chips go, and protecting model weights so they don't leak to people who'd use them for bioweapons or cyberattacks.

Chemical and biological weapons are useful because they show that the international community can stigmatize and largely restrict certain capabilities even when the underlying science is widely available. The Biological Weapons Convention isn't perfect, but there's a strong norm. And bio specifically matters because one of the most concerning near-term misuse risks of AI is that it lowers the expertise barrier for creating pathogens. So the analogy isn't just structural, it overlaps directly.

The third leg is competitiveness. States don't just want to prevent catastrophe, they want to stay strong economically and militarily. Nuclear power coexists with nuclear weapons; biotech gives us vaccines and medicine. So the frame lets you hold several things at once: deter destabilizing projects, prevent proliferation to rogue actors, and still let countries compete and benefit.

Of course, the analogies aren't perfect. AI is far more general-purpose, it's developed mostly by private companies, the inputs are harder to monitor than uranium enrichment in some ways, and AI systems can act autonomously, which a warhead never could. Loss of control has no clean nuclear analog. But I'd rather start from frameworks that worked reasonably well under real geopolitical pressure and adapt them than reason from scratch or treat AI as just another software product. Policymakers and national security people already understand these concepts, which makes them a practical bridge for getting serious about the risks.

r001.rationale: The response says these technologies are dual-use, with economic benefits and military or mass-casualty applications, and identifies that combination as their shared basis for comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing is that AI is a dual-use technology, and those are the technologies we've actually had to grapple with before as a civilization. With nuclear, the same fissile material and the same enrichment capacity gives you energy or it gives you a weapon. Chemistry gives you fertilizer and it gives you nerve agents. Biology gives you vaccines and it gives you engineered pathogens. AI is like that too, and probably more so, because it's a general-purpose amplifier of whatever you point it at. So you can't really think about it the way you'd think about, say, a consumer electronics product. You have to think about it the way states have had to think about WMD-relevant technologies.

The second thing is that these are cases where the geopolitical dynamics were actually worked out, at least partially. With nuclear, there's deterrence, there's mutual assured destruction, there's nonproliferation, there's export controls on enrichment technology, there's a whole structure of monitoring and verification. Those didn't come from nowhere, they came from people realizing that a decisive first-mover advantage with a destabilizing technology is extremely dangerous, and that you want to put yourself in a world where no one has an incentive to make a destabilizing bid for dominance. That's the structure Eric Schmidt, Alexandr Wang, and I were trying to import when we talked about mutual assured AI malfunction. If a state sees a rival racing toward something like a superintelligence that would give it a durable strategic monopoly, that rival has strong incentives to sabotage the project, through cyberattacks or otherwise. Once that's understood on all sides, you have a kind of deterrence regime, and it hopefully makes an unstable race less likely.

Nonproliferation is the other piece. We don't let just anyone acquire enriched uranium or precursor chemicals in bulk, and we have institutions like the IAEA and the OPCW that exist for that reason. The analog for AI is compute. Advanced chips are the enrichment equivalent, they're a chokepoint, they're produced in a small number of places, and you can track them. So export controls and know-your-customer on compute are the obvious lever if you want to keep catastrophic capabilities out of the hands of rogue actors, terrorists, and so on, while still letting the technology diffuse for the economically beneficial uses.

And then biology and chemistry are useful because they show you the limits of the nuclear analogy. With nuclear, the barrier is materials. With bio, the barrier is more about knowledge and expertise, and that's exactly the thing AI erodes. A model that walks a non-expert through synthesis pathways or lab troubleshooting lowers the bar in a way that nuclear tech never did. So they remind you that the threat model isn't just states, it's also a much broader set of actors, and that you need a different kind of safeguard, things at the model level rather than only at the hardware level.

So I'd say the analogies are useful partly because they're apt about the stakes, and partly because they're the only historical precedents we have for managing technologies where getting it wrong is irreversible. They're not perfect, and I try to be clear about where they break down, but they're a much better starting point than treating this as a normal tech race.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes AI and nuclear, chemical, and biological technologies as dual-use, giving examples of beneficial uses and weapons or harmful applications.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful because they show how a technology can be both economically valuable and a source of national security risk. AI isn’t just a consumer product. It can change the balance of power between states, and that means we should expect governments to care about who has access to it, who controls its supply chain, and what military advantages it provides.

Nuclear technology gives us examples of deterrence, arms races, and efforts to prevent proliferation. But the analogy has limits: nuclear weapons require materials and infrastructure that are relatively difficult to obtain and monitorable. AI is software, so once you have a capable system, distributing it can be much easier.

Biology and chemistry bring out the dual-use aspect. The same knowledge and tools can support beneficial research or enable harm. That makes governance more complicated than simply separating peaceful technology from weapons.

So I wouldn’t take any one of these as a complete model for AI. They give us different ways to think about competition, access, verification, and international cooperation. They also remind us that states can compete intensely while still having a shared interest in preventing catastrophe.

r001.rationale: The response says these technologies can be economically valuable while posing national security risks, and explicitly describes knowledge and tools serving beneficial research or enabling harm. It presents those features as reasons the technologies offer different analogies for AI geopolitics.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think they’re useful because they remind us that a technology can be economically valuable and also a source of national power and catastrophic risk. So AI isn’t necessarily going to be governed just as another consumer product. Governments will care about who controls it, who has access to it, and whether an adversary can gain a decisive advantage.

Nuclear technology gives you one picture: very concentrated capabilities, substantial barriers to entry, and a major role for states. Chemical and biological technologies give you a different picture, where the same tools and infrastructure can support beneficial work or dangerous applications. That dual-use character makes governance much harder, because you want to preserve the benefits while limiting misuse.

AI has elements of both. Developing the most capable systems can require concentrated resources, but capabilities can also spread and become easier to use. So I wouldn’t take any one analogy literally. They’re useful for thinking through different problems: competition between states, proliferation, verification, and how you get cooperation when everyone is worried about falling behind.

r001.rationale: The response clearly describes dual-use potential for chemical and biological technologies and relates it to AI, but it does not identify nuclear technology as having both beneficial and weaponized applications. That leaves the shared dual-use comparison across all three technologies incomplete.
